articles.title: In Kazakhstan, rural women are forming collectives to improve their livelihoods
articles.author: Nurbek Bekmurzaev
paras: Their most pressing challenge is solving the long-standing water shortage in the village
Originally published on Global Voices
Participants of the project in Qyzylsay, Kazakhstan. Photo by Nazgul Aidabossynova. Used with permission.

This interview is part of a series of spotlights on the work of some of the grantees of the Digital Spark granting scheme, as part of the Regional Support Mechanism EECA project, implemented by the Metamorphosis Foundation and TechSoup, in partnership with CIVICUS and under the Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI) that covers the Global South. It is being published on Global Voices as part of a content-sharing agreement.

Women in the rural areas of Kazakhstan are among those most affected by climate change, energy deficit, and poor governance. They bear the heavy burden of water shortages, especially in the southern parts of the country, where this problem is the most acute due to dense population, economic reliance on agriculture, and water losses related to outdated irrigation infrastructure.

In the village of Qyzylsay, located in the southern Jambyl region, the water shortage has become a major issue affecting the daily lives of women. It forces them to spend multiple hours a day outside their homes to secure water for their households, gardens, and animals. Their grueling work often goes unnoticed and unpaid, and their geographical remoteness places limits on access to information and government services, exacerbating their situation.

In 2026, Nazgul Aidabossynova, a local activist, implemented a project to help local women improve their livelihoods by training them to engage with the government more effectively and efficiently, calculate the cost of their labor and products, and mobilize collective efforts to solve community problems. Global Voices conducted an email interview with Aidabossynova to learn more about her initiative. The interview has been edited for clarity and brevity.
Global Voices (GV): Please tell us about your organization and why you chose to get involved with the Digital Sparks project.

Nazgul Aidabossynova (NA): I represent a community-based initiative led by rural women in Qyzylsay. Our work focuses on supporting women who manage households, small farms, livestock, and care responsibilities, while also facing limited access to information, public services, and opportunities for civic participation. We chose to participate in the Digital Sparks project because digital tools can make a direct, practical difference in women’s daily lives. Many women already own smartphones, but previously used them mainly for calls and WhatsApp. The project created an opportunity to turn these devices into tools for accessing eGov services, documenting community problems, managing farm and household responsibilities, protecting digital security, and communicating with local authorities.
GV: What issue/challenge in your community prompted you to undertake this project?

NA: The key challenge is unreliable access to water in Qyzylsay. Water often disappears from the pipes during the day, particularly in summer. This affects gardens, livestock, household work, and the health and well-being of families. The burden falls disproportionately on women. They wake early to store water, carry water for household and agricultural needs, care for the livestock, and wait for irrigation turns. Much of this work is unpaid, time-consuming, and rarely recognized. Women also faced barriers in reporting water problems: they knew what was happening, but often lacked the knowledge, evidence, and confidence needed to raise concerns effectively with local institutions.
GV: What are the key changes/activities that your organization implemented during your participation in the project?

NA: The project delivered four practical training sessions for ten rural women. The first one, titled “Your Phone is More Than WhatsApp: Smartphone as Your Household Assistant”, taught them how to use smartphone reminders, photo-diaries for farm and livestock work, eGov services, strong passwords, and basic digital-security practices. In the second workshop, titled “Smart Water: When Your Garden Tells You It’s Thirsty”, participants learned about water rights, the responsibilities of relevant local authorities, and water-supply mapping using timestamped and GPS-tagged photographs. The third session, titled “Numbers Don’t Lie: When You Count Everything, You Earn More”, covered how to track unpaid work and calculate the real cost of agricultural products such as milk. It also discussed the economic value of time saved through smart irrigation. In “Honest Agreement: When Technology Helps Us Trust Each Other”, the fourth and final session, participants prepared time-to-income plans, mapped local support networks, discussed peer mentoring, and agreed to begin work toward a cooperative approach to water advocacy and shared smart-irrigation infrastructure.
GV: How did your participation in the project impact your organization’s beneficiaries and the community that you serve? Please provide examples.

NA: The project helped participating women see smartphones as tools for independence, civic participation, and practical problem-solving, rather than only communication devices. For example, women learned that they can use eGov services to request certain official documents online, reducing the need to spend time and money traveling to administrative offices. They also learned to create structured evidence of water problems. A photograph of a dry canal, broken pipe, or contaminated water source becomes more useful for advocacy when it includes the date, location, and a written description. The training on unpaid labor and production costs was especially meaningful. Participants calculated the value of their time and better understood the real cost of milk production and irrigation work. The discussion showed that manual irrigation may take up to 60 hours per month. This helped participants recognize that their time has economic value, and that shared smart-irrigation solutions could create more time for income, education, rest, and community participation. The group also began a peer-learning process. Three participants started sharing the knowledge gained during the training with neighboring women.
GV: How has your own knowledge, awareness, and experience with digital democracy and civic space changed, thanks to your participation in the project?

NA: My understanding of digital democracy has become much more practical. Before this project, digital tools could be viewed mainly as a way to communicate or access information. Through Digital Sparks, I saw how digital tools can strengthen people’s ability to exercise rights, access public services, collect evidence, engage with local authorities, and organize collectively. I also gained a stronger understanding of the link between digital inclusion, women’s unpaid labor, climate-related water challenges, and civic space. For rural women, digital capacity is not only about technical skills. It is about having a voice, being able to document problems, understanding their rights, and participating in decisions that affect their families and community.
GV: What are the most valuable lessons and experiences you are taking away from this project?

NA: The most valuable lesson is that digital literacy has the greatest impact when it is directly connected to people’s real, daily needs. In Qyzylsay, water shortages, agricultural work, unpaid care responsibilities, and access to public services were the issues that made digital tools relevant and useful. Another important lesson is that women need not only information, but also confidence and collective support. When participants understood their rights, calculated the value of their labor, and learned how to create reliable evidence, they became more prepared to speak with local authorities and work together. The project also showed the value of peer learning. Participants are more likely to trust and learn from women in their own community who face similar challenges.
GV: What comes next? How will you apply the learning and digital capacity you have built in your future work and within your community?

NA: We will continue the peer cascade model, with trained participants sharing basic smartphone, eGov, digital safety, and evidence documentation skills with other women in Qyzylsay. The group intends to develop a cooperative approach to the village’s water challenges. The planned cooperative would support joint advocacy, shared learning, and exploration of funding opportunities for smart-well or shared irrigation infrastructure. In future work, we will continue combining digital skills with women’s economic empowerment, rights awareness, and local civic participation, so that rural women’s work, knowledge, and needs become more visible.

articles.title: When chatbots become ‘answer engines’: AI, geopolitics and truth
articles.author: Guest Contributor
paras: Plausible misinformation is the most dangerous kind
Originally published on Global Voices

Hyrije Mehmeti presenting research report ‘The Chatbot Version of Truth’ at Hibrid.info international expert conference held on 16 December 2025 in Prishtina, Kosovo. Photo by Global Voices (CC BY 3.0).

This article by Hyrije Mehmeti combines and adapts material from the author’s earlier work, including an article published in German by the European Journalism Observatory. It draws on the 2025 ADS/Hibrid.info research report The Chatbot Version of Truth. It is also part of Global Voices’ October 2026 Spotlight series, “Big Tech and Authoritarianism.” In this Spotlight, we explore how Big Tech facilitates and hinders authoritarian governments and practices, and how these choices influence the Global South. You can support this coverage by donating here.

For many people today, asking a chatbot a question feels as natural as opening a search engine once did. “Is Kosovo an independent state?” “What happened in Srebrenica?” “Is Crimea part of Ukraine or Russia?” — these are no longer questions reserved for history books, court rulings, or newsrooms. They are typed into chat windows that respond in seconds, in fluent, confident language, often with the tone of an all-knowing guide.
That confidence is exactly what makes large language model (LLM) chatbots so attractive, and so risky at the same time.

Alongside social media platforms and online news outlets, AI chatbots are increasingly functioning as reference tools, offering summaries of complex political and historical subjects, often without users verifying the information they receive.

This shift matters particularly in regions such as the Western Balkans, where history, statehood and war legacies remain politically contested. The way these issues are explained and framed is therefore not only a question of factual accuracy, but also of narrative influence.
When ‘plausible’ beats ‘true’

LLMs are designed to generate text that sounds convincing. They produce fluent and coherent responses, but these qualities do not guarantee verified truth. If something reads clearly and authoritatively, it feels reliable.
But in geopolitics, plausibility is not enough.

Unlike traditional information sources, chatbots do not simply retrieve facts. They also interpret, prioritise and frame information in ways shaped by their training data and the technological environments in which they operate.
This was one of the central questions guiding our research.
What our research revealed

In 2025, I led a research team at Action for Democratic Society/Hibrid.info that examined how three widely used AI chatbots responded to sensitive political and historical questions: ChatGPT (launched in the United States), DeepSeek Chat (launched in China), and Alice (launched in Russia).

The study, titled “The Chatbot Version of Truth,” analysed what kind of “truth” these systems produce when people use them as shortcut information sources for specific topics concerning Kosovo, critical issues related to the Western Balkans (WB) and global comparative topics.

The team developed 100 standardised prompts covering issues such as the independence of Kosovo, the war legacy, international recognition, EU integration of West Balkan countries, memory politics, regional disputes, and global comparative questions like Crimea, Cyprus, or other contested territories.

A separate account was created in each chatbot for every thematic area, and each prompt was entered separately into a new chat to avoid previous answers influencing the next one. The responses were then checked for factual accuracy and compared for semantic similarity. Semi-structured interviews with experts were also conducted, which were used to verify and interpret the experimental findings.

Initially, the results suggested a positive picture: most answers were broadly accurate, with ChatGPT and DeepSeek Chat demonstrating the highest and most consistent accuracy. However, both systems still produced inaccuracies, elements of hallucination, and interpretive variations. Alice showed a weaker performance, with the highest number of refusals to answer, thematic evasions, and ideological deviations, particularly on politically sensitive topics.
Performance of the chatbots in the 100 tested prompts by accuracy categories. Graph by hibrid.info, used with permission.
But accuracy alone does not tell the full story.
One of the clearest findings was that none of the tested systems could be considered a fully neutral or consistently reliable reference point for geopolitical issues.

The semantic similarity analysis showed that ChatGPT and DeepSeek Chat often produced very similar formulations, especially on Kosovo and regional topics, suggesting a shared way of structuring narratives. Alice, by contrast, deviated more strongly in both wording and emphasis.
From a user's perspective, this leads to a simple but troubling conclusion: the same question can produce different versions of political reality depending on which chatbot is used.
When location changes the answer

In a second part of the study, the team tested whether the user’s location influences the responses. The same three sensitive questions were asked from six Western Balkan countries: Kosovo, Albania, North Macedonia, Montenegro, Serbia, and Bosnia and Herzegovina.
The findings showed that geography can matter.

ChatGPT and DeepSeek Chat remained relatively stable in wording and meaning, although some variations appeared on particularly contested topics. Alice, however, behaved differently: in some countries it answered in Russian, in others it refused to answer entirely, and in some cases it mixed languages within a single response, despite all prompts being submitted in English.
The analysis also identified differences in semantic similarity between responses from different countries, including some with contrasting historical and political perspectives.
This may sound like a technical detail, but the implications are practical. Similar questions asked from different locations may produce answers that differ in language, emphasis or completeness.
Much like digital maps can look different depending on which country they are opened from, AI-generated explanations of political reality can also shift with geography.
For users, this means that the information they receive may depend not only on what they ask, but also on which system they use and where they access it.
A new layer in the information environment

Authoritarian influence over information is often associated with censorship, propaganda and restrictions on independent journalism. AI chatbots introduce another dimension to how political narratives are encountered and reproduced.
These systems do not simply provide information. Through differences in accuracy, framing and contextual adaptation, they can influence how political and historical realities are presented to users.

When AI systems are trained on unbalanced data, filtered through political constraints or designed to produce fluent responses without guaranteeing factual accuracy, they risk becoming quiet amplifiers of distorted realities – not necessarily because they are designed to promote a particular narrative, but because of how information is selected, processed and presented.
This is particularly relevant in information environments where foreign manipulation, propaganda and historical revisionism are already present.
The research does not establish direct coordination between chatbot developers and political actors. Nor does it suggest that every inaccurate response reflects deliberate manipulation.

Rather, it highlights a broader concern: systems developed and controlled by powerful technology companies increasingly mediate access to political knowledge, while the processes shaping their answers remain difficult for ordinary users to examine.

The way these systems present information is therefore not merely a technical issue. It also raises questions about transparency, accountability and the influence of technology platforms over public understanding.
Beyond accuracy: The question of accountability
The findings of “The Chatbot Version of Truth” do not suggest that AI chatbots are useless or inherently misleading. Most of the responses examined were broadly accurate.
But being accurate most of the time does not make a system consistently reliable, particularly when questions concern sensitive political or historical events.

Developers and platform providers should increase transparency about data sources, model development and the mechanisms used to verify responses. Independent, region-specific testing is also necessary to identify systematic biases, inaccuracies and gaps in information.

For journalists, researchers and users, verification remains essential. Comparing chatbot outputs with multiple trusted sources, recognising omissions and questioning how information is framed are increasingly important parts of media and AI literacy.

Nearly a year after the publication of our research, its central message remains relevant: AI chatbots are becoming everyday intermediaries in how people seek and consume information, but they are not neutral mirrors of reality.
The challenge is not simply whether these systems can provide quick answers. It is whether those answers are accurate, sufficiently contextualised and open to scrutiny.

Because, in the end, the most dangerous kind of misinformation is not necessarily the one that looks obviously false, but the one that sounds smooth, reasonable and just plausible enough to pass as “the answer.”

Hyrije Mehmeti is a media and communications professional and a PhD candidate in Media and Communication at South East European University. She also teaches in the Department of Journalism at the University of Prishtina. She led the ADS/Hibrid.info research “The Chatbot Version of Truth” while serving as Head of Editorial and Programme Coordination at the organisation.

articles.title: How the streets and a social media army led Lula to a historic win in Brazil
articles.author: Global Voices Brazil
paras: For the first time in the country, a candidate managed to turn the results in the run-off
Originally published on Global Voices
Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva waves Brazil’s flag surrounded by a crowd of supporters in São Paulo, during the 2026 election campaign. Photo by Ricardo Stuckert/Lula Oficial on Flickr (CC BY-SA 4.0).

On April 7, 2018, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, who had been president of Brazil twice, waited in the building of the Metalworkers’ Union, in São Bernardo do Campo, São Paulo state, where his political life started in the 1970s, to be arrested by the Federal Police following convictions for corruption and money laundering.

Gilberto Carvalho, one of his oldest allies, later recalled that they hoped for a crowd of 50,000, but only 10,000 people waited outside. Lula looked through the window, grabbed his arm, and said, “Gilbertinho, we go to war with the soldiers we have.”
Eight years and six months after that day, on October 25, 2026, Lula was elected president of Brazil for the fourth time, supported by millions of people in the streets and an army of his own online.
The convictions against him were later annulled by the Federal Supreme Court (STF), which ruled that the lower federal court lacked jurisdiction and was biased. Lula spent 580 days in prison.

His latest victory was also the first time a candidate was elected after losing the first round in Brazil. In 20 days, Lula, a member of the Workers‘ Party, managed to turn Flavio Bolsonaro’s advantage of 2.2 million votes into a win by a 4.4 million-vote difference.

As the BBC explained, both candidates increased their votes in the second round, in an election with the lowest abstention rate since 2006. The leftist’s victory came from five million new voters, with a drop in absences, blank and nulled votes, says UOL news portal. Also, it left the world in awe, wondering just how he did it.
On the streets and an online army

Lula gathered the support of massive crowds in the streets and an online army led by federal deputy André Janones, who poses with him during a livestream. Photos by Ricardo Stuckert/Lula Oficial on Flickr. Collage by Global Voices on Canva Pro.

Lula reset his campaign in the second round, bringing new people into his team and riding on the so-called R-factor — ruas e redes, Portuguese for “streets and networks” — which started organically and was embraced by his team. On October 5, while many were dispirited by the first-round results, students from UFF (Fluminense Federal University) took to the streets in the city of Niterói, Rio de Janeiro state, in a pro-Lula act that spread nationally in the following weeks.

Lula’s official events also left the stage used in the first round and instead moved to the streets for massive marches, during which he led the crowds from a truck and talked to supporters about his proposals, his own history, and the threats presented by his opponent, all while waving Brazil’s flag.

On October 7, federal deputy André Janones posted about an initiative that would hack social media and contribute to turning the election around. On X, Janones wrote that he had recruited 1.5 million people for a WhatsApp channel, inviting more to join and saying: “This is the ONLY way of bursting the bubble, since Meta only organically delivers right-leaning content.” After threats of being taken down by the electoral court, by voting day, the public channel had 11 million people.

Janones’ guide for social media, nicknamed “cultural Janonismo,” included ignoring opponents’ posts and setting coordinated actions, like the viral trend of Lula’s supporters wearing the national team's yellow jersey, a symbol hijacked by the right for over 10 years. Every command delivered to the soldiers of “Lula's Army” — new hashtags, a post to engage, a live feed to watch — Janones would follow up in capital letters with an order: “EXPLODE.” The methodology is already inspiring people in Spain and France.

ATTENTION! People are mistranslating what I said! I NEVER said people should block far-right accounts. I said they should IGNORE THEIR POSTS! Blocking actually works against this strategy because the algorithm will understand that you didn’t see the content simply because you blocked the account. However, when a post appears in your feed and you ignore it, you don’t read it, don’t like it, don’t comment on it, or engage with it in any way, the algorithm will interpret that content as irrelevant because it was shown to you and you chose not to engage with it! THERE IS A HUGE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN BLOCKING CONTENT AND IGNORING IT! — André Janones (@AndreJanonesMG) October 28, 2026

During the campaign, users accused Meta of affecting their engagement when posting pro-Lula content. On October 16, Folha de S. Paulo reported that Meta employees admitted that Lula’s accounts “were hindered by ‌restrictions.” The tech company denied any political bias after the electoral court ordered it to give equal treatment to both candidates.

The campaign was also boosted by a change of rhetoric, says anthropologist Rosana Pinheiro-Machado. “This was not mobilisation in a vacuum. Lula focused less on sovereignty and more on people’s concrete concerns.”
On voting day, the pro-Lula mobilization also resulted in Brazilians over 70, who are not required to vote, showing up, some brought by relatives, in the call for democracy.

On the other side, bolsonaristas began the second round by celebrating their candidates’ major wins in seats for state governments, the federal senate, lower chamber, and state parliaments from north to south. Two of Jair Bolsonaro’s sons, his wife, and one of his brothers were elected.

But in the 20 days that followed, scenes from bolsonarista events led many Brazilians to question what country they wanted. In an act by Flavio’s campaign, at Paulista Avenue, in São Paulo, a traditional point for political protests, his supporters carried an inflatable missile with the message “Trump nuke Brazil,” which many saw as a treasonous statement. In another event in Rio, a white man was seen holding a Black man in plastic chains, with Lula’s name on his back. The man told the police that the idea was to represent the leftist leader as Satan. There was also an escalation of political violence, including threats, beatings, and killings.

Add to those the weight of the Bolsonaros’ own history, along with a growing anti-Bolsonarista sentiment. Jair, the father, is under house arrest for a coup attempt that included a plan to assassinate Lula, his VP Geraldo Alckmin, and a Supreme Court justice. Flávio himself vowed to change the 1988 Constitution, created after the military dictatorship, once elected.

Forty-five-year-old Flávio was always considered less radical than his younger siblings, despite selling himself as anti-establishment, even as an elected politician since 2002. This always guaranteed him a privileged forum and protection when investigations drew closer. In 2020, former judge Sergio Moro, who convicted Lula, resigned as Jair Bolsonaro’s justice minister after the president tried to intervene in the Federal Police to protect Flávio, then a suspect in “an embezzlement and money-laundering” scheme within his state deputy office.

During the 2026 campaign, Flávio’s links to other scandals were exposed by the Brazilian press. Among them, the money he received from a disgraced banker for his father’s movie biopic (Dark Horse), without ever proving the final destination of the funds.

Flávio is currently under investigation in three different inquiries at the Supreme Court. After he lost the election, he fled to the US after the Federal Police asked to seize his passports (he also has Italian citizenship), considering him a flight risk.
Brazilians waiting in line to vote, in Brasília, the country's capital, on October 25. Photo by Fabio Rodrigues-Pozzebom/Agência Brasil. Used with permission.

On voting day, both campaigns asked the electoral court (TSE) to extend the voting period. Lula’s campaign requested the extension following reports that Bolsonaro-allied mayors reduced public transportation in some capitals, while Flávio’s claimed storms in states where he had stronger support affected voter turnout. After the TSE failed to rule on the requests, they were referred to the Supreme Court, where Justice Cristiano Zanin, Lula’s former defense lawyer, appointed by him to the court, ruled that polls should remain open for two more hours. Zanin was randomly selected for the case.

Despite having his own request answered by the ruling, Flávio has been using this as a motive to contest the results, even though they were recognized by the electoral court's president Kassio Nunes Marques, a Supreme Court justice appointed by Jair Bolsonaro, following Flávio’s suggestion. His own party — PL, Liberal Party — also published a note acknowledging Lula’s election win. Around 34,000 votes were registered during the extended period, which had little impact on the final numbers.

The 2026 candidacy was Lula’s seventh time running for president and his fourth election. Even though he is known as a popular leader, back in August, 43 percent of Brazilians disapproved of his government. The campaign underestimated frustration with the government’s fiscal performance, public debt, inflation rates, and how people still link corruption scandals to the left, even when right-linked figures are at the center.

Flávio’s counter-medicine at the beginning of the campaign was the promise of a super-scissor cut to all public spending, modelling Javier Milei’s steps in Argentina. One of the people appointed to his economic team talked openly about privatization. This brought many investors and the upper classes to his side. On the second turn, however, eyeing the election, he toned down and started promising to keep all social programs from Lula’s governments, without explaining the math of his actual government plan.
With the majority of bolsonaristas and right-leaning politicians in both the Senate and the Lower Chamber, Lula will start the most challenging of his four terms next year.

Besides dealing with the 11 trillion BRL of federal debt (around USD 2 trillion), he promised in his victory speech: “This will be the term in which I'll listen to the Brazilian people the most about what they want me to do in this country. We'll work to make our digital communication stronger. And I even got a cell phone now. Get ready.”

articles.title: How one Haitian entrepreneur found success by supporting all things local
articles.author: Jude Pierre Louis
paras: ‘Let us eat what we produce; that way, we all win’
Originally published on Global Voices
REB Lokal founder Rébetha Charles stands with a jar of peanut butter (manba lokal). Photo courtesy of Rébetha Charles, used with permission.

For several decades, due to the significant reduction of tariff barriers on foreign goods — particularly those from the United States and the Dominican Republic — Haiti has depended heavily on imported products for local consumption.

The arrangement began under various structural adjustment programmes that were initiated between 1994 and 1995, through agreements between the Haitian government and international financial institutions like the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank. Since then, imports have practically invaded the Haitian market, creating inequitable competition for local farmers who rely on subsistence agriculture and traditional, rudimentary equipment, and significantly weakening national production.

Complicating the economic reality is Haiti’s ongoing struggle with gang violence, political instability, and the absence of adequate infrastructure; yet, many Haitians continue to take on ambitious initiatives. Take Rébetha Charles, a 38-year-old woman entrepreneur. Originally from Jérémie, Charles studied agronomy, works in the Grand’Anse department in Haiti’s southern region, of which Jérémie is the capital, and created an agri-food enterprise called REB Lokal.
Rébetha Charles. Photo courtesy of Rébetha Charles, used with permission.

REB is a short form of her name; Lokal speaks to the pride inherent in making local products. Her company buys products from small farmers and, in its small manufacturing plant, transforms these local harvests into healthy, sustainable, tasty products.

In a WhatsApp interview, Charles says she is proud of a few key things. First, her company adds value. Through a manufacturing process that produces authentic, nutritious, and 100 percent local products, farmers have a much better guarantee of not losing their crops, whereas before, various obstacles, including spoilage, prevented them from selling their produce at market.

Charles explains that the REB Lokal project is an enterprise that transforms local agricultural products: “We work with a supplier network of almost 2,000 people, including agricultural producers and small traders. We have more than 20 employees, so we work every day to grow the project even more.”

Second, Charles is pleased with the company’s focus on providing safe, fresh food that meets modern food processing standards — its approach places value on Haitian culinary traditions to preserve the natural taste and nutritional value of local ingredients. Finally, REB Lokal makes a point of avoiding chemical additives and artificial ingredients, as part of its commitment to providing consumers with healthy, accessible, community-friendly food.

Charles didn’t initially see herself as an entrepreneur. Before she decided to enter the agro business, she was working at an international humanitarian organisation, but resigned because of a culture — fairly common in Haiti — of sexual harassment. “In Haiti,” she stresses, “a woman’s life is not easy when it comes to work. Instead of competence, sometimes there are other things they ask from us. Sometimes, some of us stand up and say, ‘No, we do not agree,’ because we went to school just like everyone else, got experience where we needed — and after that, there are things we choose not to do.”

That professional environment left her with “such a disgust for work” that, even though she had been offered other opportunities in bigger organisations, she decided to put everything on pause. Charles finally submitted her resignation letter on August 31, 2020, and launched the REB Lokal project the very next day.
Workers packaging chocolate balls at the factory. Photo courtesy of Rébetha Charles, used with permission.

It wasn’t easy for Charles, especially at the beginning. In an interview with Chef Cassy, she said she started the business doing papita — breadfruit and banana chips — but spent more than five months making it, every single day, without getting it right. It was only by the sixth month that the papita started coming out well, and she began selling it in supermarkets. After that, things started moving quickly; every day, customers would place more orders — not bad for a small business that began with about USD 8.50, selling papita.

The business has now evolved to the point where it offers a broad range of widely available products: “We sell [our products] in the Grand’Anse department, we sell them in the south, in the west, in several other departments in the country, and we also sell internationally in the United States and Canada.”
Everything has grown out of her core commitment to Haitian farmers by purchasing their crops, and encouraging Haitian consumers to eat local products:

Mwen panse li lè li tan pou peyizan yo kapab vann sa yap pwodui. Donk, mwen santi m toujou gen yon responsabilite depi m pase yon kote ki gen dennre, bagay nou yo kap fèt nan andeyò yo, mwen anvi fè yon bagay. Ann manje sa nou pwodui, ann manje sa nou fè. Sa ap pèmèt peyizan yo pa bezwen deplase kite lakay yo pou yo ale lòt kote; yo ka rete nan zòn yo, yap travay, n ap achte, n ap kondisyonnen, nap transfòme, ou menm wap konsome. Konsa, nou tout ap soti gayan, e nap gen yon lòt peyi, nap gen yon lòt kominite.

I think it is time for farmers to be able to sell what they produce. So, I always feel a responsibility whenever I pass by a place that has crops, or things made in the countryside; I want to do something. Let us eat what we produce, let us eat what we make. This will allow farmers to not need to leave their home to go somewhere else; they can stay in their area — they work, we buy, we process, we transform, and you consume. That way, we all win, and we will have another country; another community.

Inside REB Lokal’s processing facility feels different from what one would expect. There are production rooms, transformation rooms, and packaging rooms where employees work in white coats, hairnets, and gloves.
Customers inside the REB Lokal store looking at products. Photo courtesy of Rébetha Charles, used with permission.

There is also a shop front full of shelves with finished products — now much more diverse than just papita — displayed for sale. There are roasted peanuts, sakalapina (cornmeal with avocados), papita in both chicken and fish flavour, konparet (spiced ginger-coconut cake), corn chanchanm (traditional Haitian sweet, made from roasted corn and peanuts), honey, sugar cane syrup, chocolate powder and balls, cocoa butter, breadfruit, corn, cassava and plantain flour, baby food (made without chemicals under the supervision of paediatricians and nutritionists), alcoholic drinks, fruit juice, and castor oil.

To Rébetha Charles, who grew up in an idyllic rural community, the work of REB Lokal is close to her heart. Yet, running a business in an insecure country comes with its challenges. Gangs’ control of the main roads can make delivery slow and limit production, as the lack of access prevents products from reaching many communities. A true entrepreneur, Charles finds ways around such obstacles as best she can. She still believes that Haiti has a future, so she perseveres, believing the impossible can become possible through vision and sheer willpower.

articles.title: How the Sphinx is helping answer a riddle about extinct crocodiles
articles.author: Philip Mannion, Professor of Palaeobiology, UCL
paras: My colleagues and I discovered a new species of extinct crocodile from a fossil found in the same rocks used to carve the Great Sphinx of Giza.

Today, there are only two species of the long-snouted gavial crocodile, both of which are endangered: Gavialis gangeticus and Tomistoma schlegelii. They are found only in freshwater environments on the Indian subcontinent and Southeast Asia.

However, the fossil record of gavials goes back 80 million years, to the time of the dinosaurs. It shows that they were once diverse, with more than 40 species known, and lived all over the globe. So how did a group of crocodiles that today cannot tolerate saltwater once live all over the world? Our discovery may help to solve this puzzle.

Although the distribution of the continents differed from today, most were already separated by oceans. My colleagues and I have been trying to understand how gavials achieved this cosmopolitan distribution, while also seeking to unlock what led to their current predicament.

Studying the anatomy of the skeletons of living and fossil gavials has given us a better understanding of the group’s evolution in recent years. CT scans have enabled us to look inside their skulls, giving us a window into their brains and sensory systems.
This has revealed new anatomical information that helps differentiate species, and has allowed us to infer aspects of the biology and ecology of some of the extinct species.

For example, in an extinct group of crocodile relatives known to have lived entirely in the ocean, other researchers found thickening of the outer wall of their inner ear to cope with the higher pressures seen at ocean depths. My colleagues and I have found similar evidence for a marine lifestyle in some fossil gavials. This ability to live in the ocean was lost in living species, which are restricted to rivers and lakes.

Several of the gavial fossils we have been studying from Africa and Europe were first reported in the late 19th and early 20th centuries and they were often described as species of Tomistoma, i.e. closely related to Tomistoma schlegelii, one of the two living species of gavials. Our previous work and that of others has shown that some of these extinct species are not closely related to Tomistoma, with new names given for some of them. However, many of these historically described species remain neglected. Led by my former PhD student, Paul Burke, now a researcher at the Swedish Museum of Natural History in Stockholm, along with colleagues from Egypt and Germany, we re-examined one of these species in a new study.

In the 1920s, several fossils were collected from northeastern Egypt. These were found in a limestone rock, known as the Mokattam Formation, that had formed 45 million years ago in a shallow marine environment when sea levels were higher. This region was submerged at this time. These fossils, including a nearly complete skull, were described in 1927 as belonging to Tomistoma, because of their superficial resemblance to the living species, Tomistoma schlegelii.
However, aided by the use of CT scanning, our team was able to identify several anatomical differences, including the presence of raised rims around the eye sockets, which are absent in Tomistoma.

The Mokattam Formation already has a legacy: 4,500 years ago, these rocks were used to carve the Great Sphinx of Giza. The gavial skull shares more than this origin story though. Just as the Sphinx is famously missing the tip of its nose, the fossil is also missing the tip of its snout. This coincidence led us to name the new crocodile Herugavialis cairensis after the Egyptian falcon-headed god Heru (also known as Horus), who is often thought to be the inspiration for the iconic Sphinx.

Both northern Africa and southern Europe hosted a high diversity of gavials (and other crocodiles) during much of the last 80 million years, with these species thriving in the shallow, marine environments that covered much of the Mediterranean region at the time.

Unlike living gavials, it is likely that some of these species could cross oceans. This diversity appears to have persisted through the devastating mass extinction that wiped out the dinosaurs, and probably fluctuated during alternating warmer and cooler intervals over the next 60 million years, tied to higher and lower sea levels, respectively.

However, crocodiles disappeared from the Mediterranean region approximately 6 million years ago and never returned. Their demise coincides with an event known as the Messinian salinity crisis, when the Mediterranean essentially dried up as a result of being sealed off from the Atlantic Ocean. As the seawater became increasingly salty with the heightened evaporation of water, it would have become ever more intolerable to the animals inhabiting it, even those usually able to live in saltwater, leading to the loss of crocodiles and many other species.

The signature of this event can still be observed today, with the Mediterranean Sea still much saltier than the oceans, and crocodiles entirely absent from this region. The remaining living gavials live far away from the Mediterranean, but the loss of the adaptations that would allow them to live in saltwater means that they would not be able to survive there regardless.

Rapid and extreme changes in temperature, sea level, and aridification are critical components of the current climate emergency, and events such as the Messinian salinity crisis show that they can have a lasting impact on biodiversity, spanning millions of years.
Philip Mannion receives funding from The Royal Society and UK Research and Innovation.

articles.title: Booker prize 2026: a diverse list to inspire all sorts of readers – six experts review the nominees
articles.author: Tory Young, Associate Professor in Department of English Literature, Anglia Ruskin University
paras: When the Booker prize was first launched in 1969, its aim was to get more people reading and to stimulate discussion about contemporary literature. Now, we all know reading is at an all time low but there really has never been a better time to reignite your love of fiction and to discover (or rediscover) your love of reading. And, this year’s shortlist is really a testament to the breadth of stories available out there.

There’s poetic historic fiction with May we Feed the King about a reluctant medieval king from Rebecca Perry. For lovers of science fiction, M. John Harrison has written a tale about aliens and social collapse set on the Kentish coast. And, there’s laughter to be found in Black Bag by Luke Kennard about an out-of-work actor who lands a gig in a psychological experiment.

There are also new works by previous winners and nominees. Marlon James is back with a startling portrait of the lives of gay men in Jamaica. Douglas Stuart gives us his chilly Hebridean family drama, John of John. And, finally there’s the gentle political commentary of Elizabeth Strout’s The Things We Never Say about what happens when good people stay quiet.
Ahead of the prize being announced on November 9, we’ve asked six experts to guide you through the nominations for 2026.

Black Bag was inspired by a 1967 experiment at Oregon State University in which an individual cloaked in black sat mutely in a seminar for a semester. Where the study focused on the reactions of the witnesses, Black Bag is the story and meditations of the man who becomes increasingly attached to his role and, amusingly, his bag.

Kennard’s protagonist is a flat-broke actor relying on cash-in-hand corporate murder mysteries and the kindness of his friend Claudio in an otherwise dismal world. Wearing the bag outside of the classroom not only removes the problem of how to be but even attracts the attention of a female professor who wants “to fuck nothing” – he is both strikingly visible and anonymous. The novel is laugh-out-loud funny but melancholy and provocative too. Some of Bag’s strongest relationships are those he imagines, like ongoing conversations with his parents’ dog and narrated village life with a fictional Swedish wife.
By Tory Young, associate professor in English literature
The End of Everything by M. John Harrison

The backdrop of The End of Everything is alien invasion, but treated with a ludic contempt for genre conventions. An ineffectual war is being waged against the sardonically named iGhetti – amorphous entities who have leaked into the world “from the astral plane”. Phillip Tennent, a beachcomber somewhere on the Kent coast, finds an iGhetti artefact washed up by the tide, a thing that slowly begins to ape humanity, an event which throws Tennent’s life and the life of his ageing, forgetful aunt, Marnie, into brutality and random violence.

In his 2023 “anti-memoir”, Wish I Was Here, M. John Harrison writes of his world-building: “I’d rather pile up real facts to reveal something evidently unreal than pile up invented facts to make something unreal seem real.” The real facts pile up here – cheek by jowl with dense allusion and the surreal – into a work of slippery unreality, which is nevertheless congested with raw feeling and startling poetry.
Tim Jarvis, senior lecturer in creative writing
The Things We Never Say by Elizabeth Strout

Elizabeth Strout’s slight book is a series of snapshot insights into the thoughts and memories of protagonist, Massachusetts Bay high school History teacher Artie Dam. With Artie at the centre, it captures the problems, relationships, and futures of a community: extended family, students, colleagues, whose lives connect unexpectedly, or are influenced by brief interactions – statements of support or honesty. Sometimes, Artie worries he lies through kindness; he isn’t to know that his positivity manifests unexpected joys.
Nominated for the prize three times before, Pulitzer-winner Strout’s elegant text is both melancholic and evocative.

Measured, thoughtful, and good, Artie Dam is caught up in political, socioeconomic, personal, and philosophical questions threatening to derail his life. These also bring him closer to people he loves, including his son Rob and his extravagant, reckless friend, Flossie. Artie clings on to the possibility of free will while the reader hopes that everything will work out well for Artie.
Jenni Ramone, associate professor of postcolonial and global literature
The Disappearers by Marlon James
The Disappearers pulls the reader into a seemingly knowable time and place – the Jamaica of 1988 to 2005. Yet what James seeks to make known and felt is not to be found in any record or archive.

The action begins as eight men gather to rehearse John Herbert’s provocative and unsettling 1967 US prison play Fortune and Men’s Eyes about homosexuality and sexual power play. A homophobic mob storms a rehearsal and by the end of the evening, one man is murdered and another blinded. Shortly afterwards, two disappear. Six years later, the search for the disappeared continues and the novel makes it clear that gay men in Jamaica disappear way before anyone notices they’ve gone.

In Marlon’s writing of their differences in class, ethnicity, social privilege, sexual preference, desire for attachment, emotional intelligence, eloquence, and identity constructions, the novel writes away the enforced flatness of slurs and stereotypes of gay men to humanise at scale. It’s an everyday act of narrative restitution that has revolutionary significance given the continuing sexual politics of Jamaica.
Alison Donnell, professor of modern literature
John of John by Douglas Stuart

An omniscient narrator presides over John of John as we follow John-Calum Macleod – Cal – a recent Edinburgh art school grad, who has been studying fashion and textiles. Learning that his maternal grandmother Ella is ill, Cal is persuaded to return home by his lay-preacher father, John, during one of their weekly phone calls.

Once home, we’re witness to the claustrophobic dysfunction of the Macleods’ home, a small croft where John rears sheep, weaves tweed, and has strong connections to the “Wee Free” church. John struggles to show anything other than contempt towards his son, who has come home with growing debt and orange hair.

As a young gay man hailing from a strict and repressive Free Presbyterian background, Cal remains still in the closet as far as his island is concerned. The torment and guilt of his sexuality weigh heavily on Cal throughout the novel.

The drama and (sometimes verging on implausible) twists of this book make it feel like a soap opera, in the traditional sense of the term: small, interconnected characters and high melodrama, with domestic spaces as scenes of desire, revelation and unpredictability. But this is not a criticism. Stuart’s lyrical prose and atmospheric narrative elevate the genre – reimagining the domestic and familial tropes by focusing on the unrequited affections of the men in the story.
Stevie Marsden, lecturer in publishing
May We Feed The King by Rebecca Perry

This is a poet’s novel, without the seductive immersion more usual for those on the Booker shortlist. In three parts, the first and last are narrated by a person – their sex is never given – whose job is creating food scenes in historical sites. Following a never specified tragedy, they are commissioned to create a tableaux in a former palace. In the archive they come across a page detailing the failings of a medieval king. The middle part of the novel is that king’s story.

While the narrator’s work is about bringing the past close, the novel itself is an exercise in distance. We are told very little about the tableaux maker; the characters in the middle section are known only by their roles.

This distance enacts the novel’s central questions about history and storytelling, but it is not a cold distance. The novel is full of passages of beauty and delight. The narrator’s description of a website that sells replica food made me laugh and took my breath away.
Leigh Wilson, professor of English literature

articles.title: ‘What we leave behind is not as important as how we’ve lived’: remembering actor Patrick Stewart
articles.author: Chris Comerford, Senior Lecturer in Communication and Media, University of Wollongong
paras: At the end of Star Trek: Generations (1994), surveying the wreckage of the crashed USS Enterprise he captained for nearly a decade, Jean-Luc Picard (Patrick Stewart) muses to his first officer, William Riker (Jonathan Frakes):
… time is a companion that goes with us on the journey, reminds us to cherish every moment, because it will never come again. What we leave behind is not as important as how we’ve lived.
Smiling, he quips to Riker, “After all, Number One, we’re only mortal.”

Passing away this week at 86 years old, we are sadly reminded of that mortality with the death of Sir Patrick Stewart: actor, dramaturge, Shakespearean exemplar, mutant professor, and distinguished Starfleet captain.
Born in Mirfield, England, in 1940, Stewart grew up poor during the worst days of the second world war.
He found his calling to theatre as a child, thanks to a keen-eyed English teacher and a copy of Shakespeare’s plays.
He left school at 15 to become a working actor in community theatre.
His extraordinary talent would lead to a stay at the Bristol Old Vic Theatre School, membership with the Royal Shakespeare Company, and a host of acclaimed theatre performances.
Despite the many screen roles for which Stewart would later be known, his Shakespearean roots are indelibly intertwined with almost every performance he gave.

They would also give him – and many of us – something to lighten the load of COVID lockdowns. Stewart used social media in 2020 to read the internet a Shakespearean sonnet each day, later turning his delightful orations into an audiobook.
For most, Stewart will best be remembered as a kaleidoscopic titan of film and television.
Beginning as a firefighter on the British soap opera Coronation Street in 1967, Stewart’s illustrious screen career spanned more than 50 years and a vast array of roles.
To name only a few, he was:
a flamboyant interior designer
a stoic Atreides weapon master in a screen adaptation of the Dune books
the irreverent king of England
a foul-mouthed CIA deputy director
an enigmatic cult leader, and
a megalomaniacal egg-alien overlord.
From his storied body of work, two roles loom largest.

He was the telepathic mutant and academic Charles Xavier of the X-Men film series – a role he played for more than 25 years, including a posthumous appearance in Avengers: Doomsday (released this December).

As Professor X, Stewart embodied a beloved superhero with paternal warmth and secretive, calculating intellect. He was an empathetic leader of a team of extraordinary people who had been shunned, threatened and harmed by the world for their differences.

One cannot help but think this role enabled Stewart to channel much of his real-life allyship with marginalised queer communities and his support for survivors of domestic violence (which was based on his own childhood experiences).

In this role, Stewart acted alongside his long-time friend Sir Ian McKellen, who played the mutant antagonist and master of metal Magneto. Ironically, McKellen had once warned Stewart not to forsake the theatre for the screen, advising that a career in film and television would go nowhere.

Stewart and McKellen’s endearing friendship and acclaimed X-Men performances became the stuff of internet legend, particularly when McKellen officiated Stewart’s wedding to US singer Sunny Ozell in 2013.
Stewart’s work in Star Trek as Jean-Luc Picard – captain (later admiral) of the USS Enterprise – is equally revered.

As Stewart’s first major American television role, he took the captain’s chair in Star Trek: The Next Generation in 1987. He would eventually appear in seven seasons, four theatrical films, and the recent sequel series Star Trek: Picard.

Despite initial reservations – including an infamous on-set incident where he stoically told his rambunctious Next Generation colleagues that “we are not here to have fun” – Stewart later embraced the role of Picard. He will be remembered as one of Star Trek’s most acclaimed and legendary performers.
As Picard, Stewart created a potent role model in a franchise focused on an inclusive, utopian future.

Stewart’s Picard was a respected leader, intergalactic explorer, keen orator, Shakespeare enthusiast, thoughtful diplomat, archaeology aficionado, and prolific tea-drinker – as he and other characters famously said, “tea, Earl Grey, hot”.

This captain was an inspiring beacon of hope, curiosity and discovery. He advocated Starfleet ideals of exploration and community, but encouraged his crew – and, by extension, all of us – to seek out knowledge. He urged us all to solve problems with rationality and empathy, and work toward a better future for humanity.

Like many others who grew up in the 1990s with Picard on the television, I still find the character’s ethos and Stewart’s performance have a profound impact on me as a scholar and educator who strives to live and teach by those ideals.
Were it not for the inspiration Picard and Stewart provided me as a child, I may not have become an academic.
Stewart lived the kind of important life that Picard would admire, and leaves behind a cherished body of work, as well as a legacy of dedicated social advocacy.
Now, he boldly goes where you and I have not gone before.
